title: India Is Sending Its Top Trade Bodies to Washington Next Week. They're Going to Fight a $30 Billion Tariff.
excerpt: FICCI, CII, the Commerce Ministry and three industry associations will testify before the USTR on July 8, arguing that America's forced-labour findings are legally flawed and economically destructive.
body:
India is about to mount the most coordinated legal and economic challenge it has ever assembled against a proposed American tariff — and the clock is ticking.

On July 8, representatives from the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI), the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, the Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA), and the Automotive Component Manufacturers Association (ACMA) will appear before the Office of the US Trade Representative's Section 301 Committee in Washington.

Their collective message: the United States' finding that India has failed to prohibit imports of goods produced with forced labour is legally baseless, factually unsupported, and would inflict serious economic harm on both countries.

## What's Actually at Stake

The USTR proposed in early June that 60 economies, including India, face additional tariffs of up to 12.5% under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The investigation doesn't allege that Indian exports themselves are produced with forced labour. Instead, it examines whether countries have enacted and enforced bans on *importing* goods made with forced labour in third countries.

It's a subtle but consequential distinction — and one that India's representatives intend to challenge head-on.

The proposed duties are not yet final. The USTR accepted public comments through July 6, and the hearings on July 7-9 represent the last formal opportunity for affected countries and industries to make their case before a decision is taken.

The stakes are enormous. India's goods exports to the United States totalled approximately $80 billion in fiscal year 2025-26. An additional 12.5% duty across broad product categories could affect tens of billions in trade, raising costs for American manufacturers and consumers who depend on Indian inputs — from auto parts and pharmaceuticals to textiles and agricultural products.


![Confederation of Indian Industry — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/89/CII_Headquarters_New_Delhi.jpg)



> **""The proposed 12.5 per cent additional duty would raise costs for US manufacturers dependent on Indian inputs without addressing the stated policy objective," CII argues in its submission."**



## India's Legal Argument

India's Commerce Ministry has rejected the USTR's conclusions in a formal written submission, calling them based on "inadequate and insufficient evidence."

The ministry argues that India maintains a "robust domestic legal regime" that includes constitutional protections under Article 23, the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act, and four comprehensive Labour Codes enacted between 2019 and 2020. It contends that this framework meets international standards and that the USTR has not demonstrated that India's import practices burden or restrict US commerce — a statutory requirement for Section 301 action.

CII's submission goes further. The industry body argues that the USTR's own examples don't hold up. India imported no rice from Myanmar and no tobacco from Malawi during the 2021-2025 review period — two of the cases cited in the investigation. CII also notes that India imported $1.537 billion worth of American cotton between 2021 and 2025, nearly twice what it bought from China, undermining any claim that India's trade patterns encourage forced-labour supply chains.

"The proposed 12.5 per cent additional duty would raise costs for US manufacturers dependent on Indian inputs without addressing the stated policy objective," CII argues in its submission. The industry body has urged the USTR to pursue "compliance-based cooperation through the established India-US Trade Policy Forum" rather than punitive tariffs.

## The Sector-by-Sector Defence

Each industry body is mounting a targeted defence.

FICCI argues that Indian export supply chains serving the US market already operate under "well-established compliance frameworks" involving traceability, supplier due diligence, independent audits, and responsible sourcing protocols. Broad-based tariffs, it contends, would punish companies that are already compliant while disrupting supply chains that have expanded significantly.


![Ministry of Commerce — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/ab/Keizaisangyosho1.jpg)


APEDA is defending India's agricultural exports, particularly rice. Its submission states that India's rice sector "does not engage forced labour nor does it import inputs made with or using forced labour." Indian rice exports comply with recognised international standards, it argues.

ACMA, representing the auto components sector, has asked for a blanket exemption. India's automotive component industry exports billions to the US and is deeply integrated into global supply chains. The association argues that additional duties would "disrupt integrated supply chains, increase costs for US manufacturers and create sourcing uncertainty for the American automotive industry."

## The Broader Trade Context

The hearings come at a delicate moment in the India-US trade relationship. The two countries are in the late stages of negotiating an interim trade agreement — US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said in June that 99% of issues have been resolved and a deal could be finalised "within weeks."

Meanwhile, the current global tariff regime is shifting. The temporary 10% tariffs imposed by the Trump administration on all countries under Section 122 are due to expire on July 24. Washington wants Section 301 determinations completed before that deadline so the new tariffs can replace the expiring ones. If a trade deal is struck first, India could potentially negotiate relief from the Section 301 duties as part of the broader agreement.

But there is a complication. On Tuesday, the USTR announced yet another round of additional tariffs — 10% to 12.5% — on imports from 60 economies related to forced labour, with India again on the list. President Trump separately stated that a trade deal with India would come "soon."

For India, the strategy is clear: fight the Section 301 case on its legal merits while simultaneously pushing to close the bilateral trade deal before the tariffs take effect. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal's team has been engaged in parallel on both fronts.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For Indian Americans, the forced-labour tariff saga is about far more than trade percentages. The broader India-US trade relationship is the foundation on which immigration policies, student visa frameworks, and technology cooperation agreements are built. A deterioration in trade ties — or the perception that India is being unfairly targeted — could ripple into other areas of the bilateral relationship.

More directly, Indian-origin professionals working in sectors like automotive manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, and IT-enabled services could feel the impact if tariffs disrupt the supply chains their employers depend on. And Indian-American entrepreneurs importing goods from India would face immediate cost increases.

The July 8 hearings will be closely watched in New Delhi, Washington, and across the diaspora. India has never before sent this many representatives to a single Section 301 proceeding. The scale of the mobilisation signals how seriously the government and industry are taking the threat — and how much is riding on the outcome.
